rule: The gain or loss is the dollars you receive minus the dollar cost (basis) of the RMB you give up. The money itself is not income again.
official_words: 'Exchange gain realized from the sale or other disposition of nonfunctional currency shall be the excess of the amount realized over the adjusted basis of such currency, and exchange loss realized shall be the excess of the adjusted basis of such currency over the amount realized.' — 26 CFR 1.988-2(a)(2)(i)

rule: The dollars the bank actually pays you are the amount realized.
official_words: 'The amount realized from the sale or other disposition of property shall be the sum of any money received' — 26 U.S.C. 1001(b)

rule: For a U.S. individual the dollar is the functional currency, so RMB is a nonfunctional currency, and converting it to dollars is a disposition of that currency.
official_words: 'the term "functional currency" means— (A) except as provided in subparagraph (B), the dollar' — 26 U.S.C. 985(b)(1). 'The conversion of the 10,000 Canadian dollars to U.S. dollars is a section 988 transaction' — 26 CFR 1.988-1(a)(6) Example 2

rule: A bank deposit in RMB counts as the currency itself.
official_words: 'the term "nonfunctional currency" includes coin or currency, and nonfunctional currency denominated demand or time deposits or similar instruments issued by a bank or other financial institution' — 26 U.S.C. 988(c)(1)(C)(ii)

rule: Depositing RMB, withdrawing RMB, or moving RMB from one RMB deposit to another is not a taxable moment. The dollar cost travels with the money.
official_words: 'No exchange gain or loss is recognized with respect to the following transactions— … (E) The transfer of nonfunctional currency from a demand or time deposit … to another demand or time deposit or similar instrument denominated in the same nonfunctional currency … The taxpayer's basis in the units of nonfunctional currency … received in the transaction shall be the adjusted basis of the units … transferred.' — 26 CFR 1.988-2(a)(1)(iii)

rule: Paying for property with RMB is treated as selling the RMB for dollars that day and then buying the property with the dollars.
official_words: 'the exchange of nonfunctional currency for property (other than nonfunctional currency) shall be treated as— (1) An exchange of the units of nonfunctional currency for units of functional currency at the spot rate on the date of the exchange, and (2) The purchase or sale of the property for such units of functional currency.' — 26 CFR 1.988-2(a)(2)(ii)(B)

rule: Each conversion is worked out on its own. A loss on one is not netted into another by this rule.
official_words: 'the amount of exchange gain or loss from a section 988 transaction shall be separately computed for each section 988 transaction, and such amount shall not be integrated with gain or loss recognized on another transaction' — 26 CFR 1.988-1(e)

rule: Investment or business money: the gain is ordinary income and the loss is an ordinary loss.
official_words: 'any foreign currency gain or loss attributable to a section 988 transaction shall be computed separately and treated as ordinary income or loss (as the case may be)' — 26 U.S.C. 988(a)(1)(A)

rule: Personal money: the ordinary-income rule above does not apply at all.
official_words: 'The preceding provisions of this section shall not apply to any section 988 transaction entered into by an individual which is a personal transaction.' — 26 U.S.C. 988(e)(1)

rule: The test: a transaction is personal unless, and only to the extent that, the expenses that belong to it would be deductible as business expenses (section 162) or as expenses of producing income (section 212).
official_words: 'the term "personal transaction" means any transaction entered into by an individual, except that such term shall not include any transaction to the extent that expenses properly allocable to such transaction meet the requirements of— (A) section 162 (other than traveling expenses described in subsection (a)(2) thereof), or (B) section 212 (other than that part of section 212 dealing with expenses incurred in connection with taxes).' — 26 U.S.C. 988(e)(3); the same test is in 26 CFR 1.988-1(a)(9)(i)

rule: The regulation gives one example on each side: pounds bought to buy a bond are inside section 988; pounds spent on a holiday are outside it. A savings balance is not addressed by name.
official_words: Example 1: 'These transactions are not excluded from the definition of a section 988 transaction … because expenses properly allocable to such transactions meet the requirements of section 212.' Example 2: 'The expenses properly allocable to such dispositions do not meet the requirements of section 162 or 212. Thus, the disposition of the pounds by X on his vacation are not section 988 transactions.' — 26 CFR 1.988-1(a)(9)(ii)

rule: Personal money, small gain: a gain of $200 or less on a transaction is not recognized. If the gain is more than $200 the exclusion does not apply to any of it.
official_words: 'no gain shall be recognized for purposes of this subtitle by reason of changes in exchange rates after such currency was acquired by such individual and before such disposition. The preceding sentence shall not apply if the gain which would otherwise be recognized on the transaction exceeds $200.' — 26 U.S.C. 988(e)(2)

rule: Personal money, gain over $200: the IRS says to report it as a capital gain.
official_words: 'If you have a gain on a personal foreign currency transaction because of changes in exchange rates, you don't have to include that gain in your income unless it's more than $200. If the gain is more than $200, report it as a capital gain.' — IRS Publication 525 (2025)

rule: A capital gain is long-term when the asset was held for more than one year; a short-term gain is taxed at ordinary rates.
official_words: 'The term "long-term capital gain" means gain from the sale or exchange of a capital asset held for more than 1 year' — 26 U.S.C. 1222(3). 'Net short-term capital gains are subject to taxation as ordinary income at graduated tax rates.' — IRS Topic no. 409

rule: An individual may deduct only three kinds of loss: a business loss, a loss on a transaction entered into for profit, and a casualty or theft loss. The IRS says losses on personal-use property are not deductible.
official_words: 'In the case of an individual, the deduction under subsection (a) shall be limited to— (1) losses incurred in a trade or business; (2) losses incurred in any transaction entered into for profit, though not connected with a trade or business; and (3) … losses of property … if such losses arise from fire, storm, shipwreck, or other casualty, or from theft.' — 26 U.S.C. 165(c). 'Losses from the sale of personal-use property, such as your home or car, aren't tax deductible.' — IRS Topic no. 409

rule: Claiming section 988 losses of $50,000 or more in one tax year makes the conversion a reportable 'loss transaction' for an individual; reportable transactions are disclosed on Form 8886.
official_words: 'A loss transaction is any transaction resulting in the taxpayer claiming a loss under section 165 of at least— … (E) $50,000 in any single taxable year for individuals or trusts … if the loss arises with respect to a section 988 transaction' — 26 CFR 1.6011-4(b)(5)(i). 'Use Form 8886 to disclose information for each reportable transaction in which you participated.' — IRS, About Form 8886

rule: Leaving out that disclosure carries its own penalty: 75% of the tax saved, not less than $5,000 and not more than $10,000 for a natural person.
official_words: '75 percent of the decrease in tax shown on the return as a result of such transaction' … 'in the case of any other reportable transaction, $50,000 ($10,000 in the case of a natural person)' … 'shall not be less than $10,000 ($5,000 in the case of a natural person)' — 26 U.S.C. 6707A(b)

rule: The dollar cost of currency follows the ordinary basis rules of the Code: cost, or the special rules for inherited and gifted property.
official_words: 'the adjusted basis of nonfunctional currency is determined under the applicable provisions of the Internal Revenue Code (e.g., sections 1011 through 1023)' — 26 CFR 1.988-2(a)(2)(iii)(A). 'The basis of property shall be the cost of such property' — 26 U.S.C. 1012(a)

rule: RMB taken out of a bank account: use any reasonable method, the same one every year and for every foreign-currency account. First in first out, last in first out and pro rata are named. A method that always takes the highest-cost RMB first is not allowed.
official_words: 'The basis of nonfunctional currency withdrawn from an account with a bank or other financial institution shall be determined under any reasonable method that is consistently applied from year to year by the taxpayer to all accounts denominated in a nonfunctional currency. For example, a taxpayer may use a first in first out method, a last in first out method, a pro rata method (as illustrated in the example below), or any other reasonable method that is consistently applied. However, a method that consistently results in units of nonfunctional currency with the highest basis being withdrawn first shall not be considered reasonable.' — 26 CFR 1.988-2(a)(2)(iii)(B)(1)

rule: The regulation's own example: an account holding 1,200 Swiss francs with a total cost of $600; 500 francs are withdrawn; pro rata, their cost is $250 and $350 stays with the rest.
official_words: 'X's basis in the 500 Swiss francs is $250 … X's basis in the Swiss francs remaining in the account is $350 ($600−$250). X must use this method consistently from year to year with respect to withdrawals of nonfunctional currency from all of X's accounts.' — 26 CFR 1.988-2(a)(2)(iii)(B)(2)

rule: Income received in RMB is translated into dollars at the rate on the day it is received; that dollar figure is what the RMB cost.
official_words: 'you must immediately translate into dollars all items of income, expense, etc. … that you receive, pay, or accrue in a foreign currency … Use the exchange rate prevailing when you receive, pay, or accrue the item.' — IRS, Foreign currency and currency exchange rates. 'The acquisition of nonfunctional currency is treated as a section 988 transaction for purposes of establishing the taxpayer's basis in such currency' — 26 CFR 1.988-1(a)(1)

rule: Bank interest credited in RMB is translated at the rate on the day received, or by one consistent convention such as month-end; crediting it creates no currency gain.
official_words: 'Interest income received with respect to a demand account … shall be translated into functional currency at the spot rate on the date received or accrued or pursuant to any reasonable spot rate convention consistently applied … No exchange gain or loss is realized upon the receipt or accrual of interest income with respect to a demand account' — 26 CFR 1.988-2(b)(1)

rule: RMB received for selling property takes its dollar cost on the day it is received (for listed securities sold by a cash-basis taxpayer, the settlement date). The currency clock starts then.
official_words: 'The acquisition of the 100,000 krone on January 1, 1989, and the acquisition of the 120,000 krone on August 1, 1989, are section 988 transactions for purposes of establishing the basis of such krone.' — 26 CFR 1.988-1(a)(6) Example 8. 'X's basis in the £110 received from the sale of the stock is $166.' — 26 CFR 1.988-2(a)(2)(iv)(C)

rule: Inherited property takes its value at the date of death.
official_words: 'the basis of property in the hands of a person acquiring the property from a decedent … shall … be— (1) the fair market value of the property at the date of the decedent's death' — 26 U.S.C. 1014(a)

rule: Gifted property keeps the giver's cost; for working out a loss, the value on the day of the gift is used if it is lower.
official_words: 'the basis shall be the same as it would be in the hands of the donor … except that if such basis … is greater than the fair market value of the property at the time of the gift, then for the purpose of determining loss the basis shall be such fair market value' — 26 U.S.C. 1015(a)

rule: The IRS has no official rate and accepts any posted rate used consistently. The regulation names Federal Reserve, IMF and published daily rates as acceptable evidence of the spot rate.
official_words: 'The Internal Revenue Service has no official exchange rate. Generally, it accepts any posted exchange rate that is used consistently.' — IRS, Yearly average currency exchange rates. '… exchange rates published by the Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System pursuant to 31 U.S.C. section 5151; exchange rates published in newspapers, financial journals or other daily financial news sources' — 26 CFR 1.988-1(d)(1)

rule: Where an official rate and a free-market rate differ, the rate that most clearly reflects income is used.
official_words: 'If a currency has an official government established rate that differs from a free market rate, the spot rate shall be the rate which most clearly reflects the taxpayer's income. Generally, this shall be the free market rate.' — 26 CFR 1.988-1(d)(4)(i)

rule: Ordinary income is taxed at seven rates from 10% to 37%; the 2026 brackets are in the table on this page.
official_words: 'The existing seven tax rates of 10%, 12%, 22%, 24%, 32%, 35%, and 37% remain in effect for individual taxpayers.' — Rev. Proc. 2025-32, section 2.01; tables in section 4.01

rule: A long-term capital gain is taxed at 0%, 15% or 20% depending on taxable income; the 2026 limits are in the table on this page.
official_words: 'Net capital gains are taxed at different rates depending on overall taxable income, although some or all net capital gain may be taxed at 0%.' — IRS Topic no. 409. 'the maximum zero rate amounts and maximum 15 percent rate amounts' — Rev. Proc. 2025-32, section 4.03

rule: A further 3.8% applies to net investment income once modified adjusted gross income passes $200,000 (single or head of household), $250,000 (joint) or $125,000 (married filing separately). The statute counts net gain from the disposition of property; whether a currency gain is inside that is not stated by name.
official_words: 'a tax equal to 3.8 percent of the lesser of— (A) net investment income for such taxable year, or (B) the excess (if any) of— (i) the modified adjusted gross income for such taxable year, over (ii) the threshold amount' … 'net gain (to the extent taken into account in computing taxable income) attributable to the disposition of property' — 26 U.S.C. 1411(a)(1), (c)(1)(A)(iii)

rule: A section 988 gain is sourced to the country of the individual's tax home; with no tax home, a U.S. citizen is treated as resident in the United States.
official_words: 'the source of such amount shall be determined by reference to the residence of the taxpayer' … 'in the case of an individual, the country in which such individual's tax home (as defined in section 911(d)(3)) is located' … 'If an individual does not have a tax home (as so defined), the residence of such individual shall be the United States if such individual is a United States citizen or a resident alien' — 26 U.S.C. 988(a)(3)

rule: The IRS may treat a transaction, or a series of them, as a section 988 transaction when its effect is to avoid section 988.
official_words: 'The Commissioner may recharacterize a transaction (or series of transactions) in whole or in part as a section 988 transaction if the effect of such transaction (or series of transactions) is to avoid section 988.' — 26 CFR 1.988-1(a)(11)(i)

rule: A capital gain is reported on Form 8949 and Schedule D. The line for an ordinary section 988 gain or loss was not found on an official page.
official_words: 'Report most sales and other capital transactions and calculate capital gain or loss on Form 8949, Sales and Other Dispositions of Capital Assets, then summarize capital gains and deductible capital losses on Schedule D (Form 1040).' — IRS Topic no. 409
